title: Week 2: dplyr and Census Data
text:
Key Concepts

saving result in R
result <- filter(counties, population > 5000)


packages
install.packages("dplyr")
library(dplyr)


Data frames and dplyr
Main verbs: - filter() — choose rows based on conditions. - select() — choose columns. - mutate() — add or modify computed columns. - arrange() — sort rows; use desc() for descending order. - group_by() + summarize() — calculate statistics by group, similar to SQL aggregation.


Pipelines
new_data <- counties |>
  filter(moe_pct > 10) |>
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) |>
  select(name, moe_pct)


Getting ACS data
library(tidycensus)

data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c("VARIABLE_ID_1", "VARIABLE_ID_2"),
  state = "PA",
  year = 2014,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)


GEOIDs
Treat GEOIDs as strings, not numbers, so leading zeros are preserved. Typical components: - State: 2 digits - County: 3 digits - Census tract: 6 digits - Block group: 1 additional digit when applicable A state + county + tract GEOID is usually 11 digits.

text:
What this means for policy
[Your 200–250 word reflection goes here.]
Among California counties, Alpine and Sierra have the greatest relative uncertainty in their median age estimates. Alpine County has an estimated median age of 41.1 years and a margin of error (MoE) of 4.8 years (11.68% of the estimate). Sierra County has an estimated median age of 56 years and a MoE of 5 years (8.93%). Both are measured less precisely than other counties.
Using relative MOE cutoffs of 0.5% and 1%, the 16 high-confidence counties average roughly 1,711,758 residents, compared with 25,185 for the 16 low-confidence counties. The 26 moderate-confidence counties average 440,450. This pattern reflects how the ACS works: it surveys a sample of residents, and smaller counties yield fewer observations, so their estimates carry more uncertainty.
Suppose a state agency used median age to prioritize funding for older-adult services. An underestimated median age might cause a county to miss support; an overestimate might divert funding from communities that need it. Alpine and Sierra would be especially exposed to such errors. Agencies should weigh MoE alongside point estimates — and recognize that median age alone does not capture the number of older residents who need services.

Optional challenges - For those craving more
Using 2023 ACS five-year estimates, I compared the precision of median age estimates for Los Angeles County and its census tracts. The county’s relative MOE was 0.26%, while the median relative MOE across 2,477 valid tracts was 10.12%. Another 21 tracts were excluded for missing estimates.
With reliability thresholds at 5% and 10%, 181 tracts (7.31%) fell into high confidence, 1,037 (41.87%) into moderate, and 1,259 (50.83%) into low confidence.
A precise county estimate does not guarantee equally precise estimates at the tract level. Smaller areas yield fewer survey observations and more uncertainty. Agencies directing older-adult services to specific neighborhoods should check tract-level MOEs rather than relying on county precision alone.

Key Concepts

Anscombe’s Quartet
The four datasets have the same or nearly identical mean x, mean y, correlation, and regression line, but very different distributions when plotted.


How to Build a ggplot

Step 1: Assign an object and create a blank canvas
p <- ggplot(data)

# You can also start without specifying data
p <- ggplot()


Step 2: Define aesthetic mappings
aes() maps data to visual properties such as position and color.

Inside aes(): map a variable or category to a visual property.
Outside aes(): set a visual property to a fixed value.

# Map the category "blue" to color.
# This creates a legend labeled "blue";
# it does not necessarily make the points blue.
ggplot(county_data) +
  aes(x = estimate, y = moe_pct, color = "blue") +
  geom_point()

# Set all points to blue
ggplot(county_data) +
  aes(x = estimate, y = moe_pct) +
  geom_point(color = "blue")

# Color points according to the city variable
ggplot(df, aes(x = income, y = rent)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = city))


Step 3: Choose a geometry



Function
Purpose




geom_histogram()
Show the distribution of a variable


geom_point()
Show the relationship between two variables


geom_boxplot()
Compare distributions across groups


geom_col()
Compare values across groups


geom_line()
Show changes over time


geom_errorbar()
Display uncertainty



p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = income, y = rent, color = city)) +
  geom_point()
The + operator adds layers or other plot components.



ACS Error and Reliability

Standard Error (SE)
For an ACS margin of error reported at the 90% confidence level:
\[
SE = \frac{MOE}{1.645}
\]


Coefficient of Variation (CV)
\[
CV = \frac{SE}{\text{Estimate}} \times 100%
\]
CV thresholds from the class notes:



CV Level
Range
Interpretation




Low
< 15%
High reliability


Medium
15%–30%



High
> 30%
High sampling error





Uncertainty in Derived Estimates
When calculating sums, proportions, or ratios, account for uncertainty in the original estimates. Both the numerator and denominator may have sampling error.








Function
Purpose
Example




moe_sum()
Calculate the MOE of a sum
Add populations across several areas


moe_prop()
Calculate the MOE of a part-to-whole proportion
Population in poverty ÷ population for whom poverty status is determined


moe_ratio()
Calculate the MOE of a general ratio
Number of jobs ÷ number of housing units





Changes Over Time
When comparing ACS multiyear estimates, use periods with non-overlapping years.
Convert each period’s MOE to its standard error:
\[
SE_1 = \frac{MOE_1}{1.645},
\qquad
SE_2 = \frac{MOE_2}{1.645}
\]
Assuming the two estimates are independent, the standard error of the difference is:
\[
SE_{\text{diff}} = \sqrt{SE_1^2 + SE_2^2}
\]
Define the difference as:
\[
\text{Difference} = \text{Estimate}_1 - \text{Estimate}_2
\]
The Z-score is:
\[
Z = \frac{\text{Estimate}_1 - \text{Estimate}2}{SE{\text{diff}}}
\]
The 90% confidence interval for the change is:
\[
\text{Difference} \pm 1.645 \times SE_{\text{diff}}
\]

title: Verify the Claim: Did Philadelphia’s Poverty Rate Change Significantly?
text:
Read the origin report.
I examine whether poverty rates in Philadelphia changed significantly between the 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 ACS five-year periods. I use census tract estimates from Census Bureau Table B17001, “Poverty Status in the Past 12 Months by Sex by Age.” Specifically, I use the population for whom poverty status is determined (B17001_001) as the denominator and the population below the poverty level (B17001_002) as the numerator. The two periods do not overlap.
The following hypothesis is made:
\(\text{H}_0\): The poverty rate in tracts of Philadelphia is not changed from 2010 to 2017.


Show code
library(tidycensus)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(gt)

# H0: The poverty rate in tracts of Philadelphia is not changed from 2010 to 2017.

acs_list <- c("B17001_001", "B17001_002")

format_poverty <- function(df){
  df %>%
  mutate(
    variable = recode(
      variable,
      "B17001_001" = "Total Population",
      "B17001_002" = "Population in Poverty"
    )
  )%>%
    pivot_wider(
      id_cols = c(GEOID, NAME),
      names_from = variable,
      values_from = c(estimate, moe),
      names_glue = "{variable}_{.value}",
      names_vary = "slowest"
    )
}

poverty_2010 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = acs_list,
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  year = 2010,
  survey = "acs5"
) %>%
  format_poverty()

poverty_2017 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = acs_list,
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  year = 2017,
  survey = "acs5"
) %>%
  format_poverty()

Code
The following code provide info for later discussion.


Show code
poverty <- poverty_2010 %>%
  inner_join(
    poverty_2017,
    by = c("GEOID", "NAME"),
    suffix = c("_2010", "_2017")
  )


poverty_withrate <- poverty %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_rate_2010 =
      `Population in Poverty_estimate_2010` /
      na_if(`Total Population_estimate_2010`, 0),

    poverty_rate_moe_2010 = tidycensus::moe_prop(
      num = `Population in Poverty_estimate_2010`,
      denom = na_if(`Total Population_estimate_2010`, 0),
      moe_num = `Population in Poverty_moe_2010`,
      moe_denom = `Total Population_moe_2010`
    ),

    poverty_rate_2017 =
      `Population in Poverty_estimate_2017` /
      na_if(`Total Population_estimate_2017`, 0),

    poverty_rate_moe_2017 = tidycensus::moe_prop(
      num = `Population in Poverty_estimate_2017`,
      denom = na_if(`Total Population_estimate_2017`, 0),
      moe_num = `Population in Poverty_moe_2017`,
      moe_denom = `Total Population_moe_2017`
    )
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    cv_2010 = poverty_rate_moe_2010 / 1.645 / poverty_rate_2010 * 100,
    cv_2017 = poverty_rate_moe_2017 / 1.645 / poverty_rate_2017 * 100
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    delta_p = poverty_rate_2017 - poverty_rate_2010,
    delta_moe = sqrt(poverty_rate_moe_2010^2 + poverty_rate_moe_2017^2)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    max_p = delta_p + delta_moe,
    min_p = delta_p - delta_moe,
    include_zero = ifelse(min_p <= 0 & max_p >= 0, TRUE, FALSE)
  )

  slice_head(n = 15) %>%

  geom_col(aes(x = reorder(NAME, delta_p), y = delta_p, fill = include_zero)) +

  coord_flip() +
  labs(

Findings
Of the 376 testable census tracts, 36 showed statistically significant increases in poverty rates and 27 showed significant decreases at the 90% confidence level. title: Week 4: Go Spatial!
text:
Key Concepts

table join

inner_join(): Keep matching records only.
left_join(): Keep all left-table records; unmatched values become NA.
full_join(): Keep all records from both tables.



Spatial Data and CRS

get_acs(..., geometry = TRUE): Return census data with spatial geometry.
Sticky geometry: Geometry stays attached during table operations; remove with st_drop_geometry().
CRS: Defines how coordinates represent locations.
Geographic CRS: Longitude and latitude, measured in degrees.
Projected CRS: Planar coordinates, usually measured in meters or feet.
NAD83: Common datum for North American data.
WGS84: Global datum used by GPS.



Map Projections

Types: Cylindrical, conic, and planar/azimuthal.
Conformal: Preserves local angles and shapes.
Equal-area: Preserves area.
Equidistant: Preserves distances along specific lines or from specific points.
Azimuthal: Preserves directions from a central point.
UTM: Uses 60 zones and meter-based coordinates, normally positive within the appropriate zone.



Essential sf Functions







Function
Key purpose




st_crs(x)
Check the CRS


st_set_crs(x, crs)
Assign a CRS label without changing coordinates


st_transform(x, crs)
Convert coordinates to another CRS


st_buffer(x, dist)
Create a buffer


st_intersects(x, y)
Test whether geometries share any location


st_touches(x, y)
Test whether geometries touch without interior overlap


st_within(x, y)
Test whether x lies within y


st_filter(x, y)
Keep features based on a spatial relationship


st_union(x)
Merge geometries and dissolve internal boundaries


st_join(x, y)
Join attributes based on spatial relationships


st_distance(x, y)
Calculate distances between geometries

title: Week 5: Machine Learning & Linear Regression
text:
Key Concepts

1. Goal of Machine Learning

In this class, ML is used mainly for prediction: producing accurate predictions on new data.
This differs from inference in traditional statistics, which focuses on understanding and explaining relationships between variables.



2. Basic Model Form
\[y = f(x) + \epsilon\] - \(f(x)\): the systematic relationship between \(X\) and \(y\). The model’s job is to estimate \(\hat{f}\). - \(\epsilon\): random error with mean 0. This is the irreducible error. - Prediction error = reducible error (from imperfect estimation of \(f\)) + irreducible error (\(\epsilon\)).


3. Model Flexibility Spectrum: Rigid → Flexible
Linear → Lasso / Ridge → Logistic → Tree-based → Boosting → Neural Network









Direction
Flexibility
Interpretability
Risk




Left (rigid)
Low
High
Underfitting (high bias)


Right (flexible)
High
Low (black box)
Overfitting (high variance)




Lasso (L1): shrinks some coefficients exactly to 0, so it performs variable selection.
Ridge (L2): shrinks all coefficients toward 0 without setting any to 0. Useful when predictors are collinear.
Logistic: used for binary classification. It outputs probabilities.



4. Parametric vs. Non-parametric

Parametric models assume a functional form for \(f\) (e.g., linear) and then estimate its parameters. They are simple, interpretable, and need less data, but they have high bias if the assumed form is wrong.
Non-parametric models assume no fixed form for \(f\) (e.g., trees, KNN). They are highly flexible but need more data and are prone to overfitting.



5. Linear Regression
\[\hat{y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots + \beta_p x_p\] - \(\beta_0\): the intercept. - \(\beta_1\): the average change in \(y\) for a one-unit increase in \(x_1\), holding other variables constant. It gives the direction and size of \(x_1\)’s influence.

Least Squares (OLS)

Coefficients are estimated by minimizing the residual sum of squares (RSS): \[\min_{\beta} \; RSS = \sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\]




6. Evaluation Metrics

\(R^2\): the proportion of variance in \(y\) explained by the model. It ranges from 0 to 1, and higher is better. \[R^2 = 1 - \frac{RSS}{TSS}\]

Note: \(R^2\) always increases when you add variables, so also check Adjusted \(R^2\) or out-of-sample performance.

RMSE: the typical size of prediction errors, in the same units as \(y\). Lower is better. \[RMSE = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}\]

For prediction tasks, focus on test-set or CV RMSE.




7. Cross Validation (CV)

Purpose: estimate how the model performs on unseen data, compare models, and tune parameters.
K-Fold CV:

Randomly split the data into K folds.
Train on K−1 folds and validate on the remaining fold.
Repeat K times and average the error (e.g., mean RMSE).

The exercises use K = 10. K = 5 or 10 is a common balance between bias and variance.



8. Over-fitting

An overfit model learns the noise in the training data, so training error is low but test error is high.
More flexible models overfit more easily. This is the bias–variance trade-off.
Remedies: select models with CV, use regularization (Lasso/Ridge), reduce the number of variables, or get more data.



9. Multicollinearity

Multicollinearity means the predictors are highly correlated with each other.
Consequences: unstable coefficient estimates, inflated standard errors, and coefficient signs or magnitudes that are hard to interpret. Prediction accuracy is usually less affected.
Diagnosis: check the correlation matrix or VIF (above 5 or 10 is considered severe).
Remedies: drop or combine variables, use Ridge, or apply PCA.



10. Homoscedasticity

Given all predictors \(X\), the variance of the error term is constant: \[\operatorname{Var}(\epsilon_i \mid X) = \sigma^2 \quad (\text{constant})\]
When this fails, the errors are heteroscedastic. Standard errors become biased, so significance tests are unreliable.
Diagnosis: plot residuals vs. fitted values (a funnel shape signals heteroscedasticity), or run the Breusch–Pagan test.
Remedies: log-transform \(y\), use robust standard errors, or use weighted least squares (WLS).

ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {

Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
Many of the city’s datasets on OpenDataPhilly are served through a Carto SQL API. You send a SQL query in a URL, and it sends back data. Ask for format=GeoJSON and st_read() reads the result directly, just like the Indego feed in Week 4.
The pattern:
https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=SELECT ... FROM table_name WHERE ...
Three pieces of SQL are all you need:

SELECT the_geom, column1, column2 chooses which columns come back. Always include the_geom, or you get no geometry.
FROM table_name chooses the dataset.
WHERE ... filters rows. Filter in the query, not in R. Some tables have millions of rows, and pulling everything will be slow or fail.

This helper builds the URL for you. Spaces and symbols in a URL need encoding, and URLencode() handles that.


Code
carto_get <- function(sql) {
  url <- paste0("https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=", URLencode(sql))
  st_read(url, quiet = TRUE)
}

4B: Density: don’t skip this
Raw counts mostly measure tract size. A big tract has more of everything. Normalize by area, by population, or by housing units, depending on what makes sense for the thing you’re counting.

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    area_sqmi         = as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 27878400,   # sq ft in a sq mile
    burglary_per_sqmi = n_burglary / area_sqmi,
    burglary_per_1k   = n_burglary / total_popE * 1000
  )








NotePer capita in low-population tracts



If a tract has 40 residents and 3 burglaries, its rate is 75 per 1,000, which is a huge number built on tiny counts. Look at the tracts with the highest per-capita rates before you trust them. This is the Week 3 lesson about small denominators again.




4C: Measuring distance to the nearest thing
How far is each tract from its nearest Indego station? Use the Week 4 pattern: find the nearest feature, then measure to it element by element.

stations <- st_read("https://www.rideindego.com/stations/json/", quiet = TRUE) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

nearest_idx <- st_nearest_feature(tract_pts, stations)

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_station_mi = as.numeric(
    st_distance(tract_pts, stations[nearest_idx, ], by_element = TRUE)) / 5280)

Sometimes the “thing” is a single location, such as City Hall as a stand-in for the center of the regional economy.

Part 5: Transforming features
Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before you start this part. Below is a summary to work from.
So far, every predictor has entered the model as a straight line: each additional unit of X changes predicted Y by the same amount, everywhere. Transformations let the model bend. For prediction, the question is simply does the bend lower CV RMSE? For interpretation, each transformation changes what a coefficient means, so you need to know how to read it.






TipTransform predictors, not your outcome



Keep your outcome y untransformed in this assignment. If you model log(y), your CV RMSE comes out in log units and can’t be compared to the other rows in your log. (Predicting a logged outcome well requires back-transforming, which is an A4 topic.)



5A: Logs, for skewed predictors
Many urban variables are skewed: a few tracts have huge values, and most have small ones. Income, density, and counts are typical. A log compresses the long tail, so a model can use the difference between 1 and 10 as well as the difference between 100 and 1,000.


Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = burglary_per_sqmi)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()









Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = log1p(burglary_per_sqmi))) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()















Warninglog(0) doesn’t exist



log(0) is -Inf, and it will break your model. Counts and densities often include zeros. Use log1p(x), which computes log(x + 1), for anything that can be 0.


Reading the coefficient: when a predictor is logged, a 1% increase in X goes with a change of about β/100 in Y, in Y’s units. With log1p, this reading is approximate for small values of X.


5B: Squared terms, for curves
If your scatterplot bends (rising and then flattening, or falling and then rising), a squared term lets the line curve. Write it with I(), which tells R to do the arithmetic rather than read ^ as formula syntax.

Sometimes a number works better as groups, either because the relationship isn’t smooth or because the categories are meaningful. You can make categories from any variable with case_when() or cut(), and then make sure R treats them as a factor.

text:
Part 7: Reflection (about 300 words)
Answer in prose, drawing on your model log (incorporate our words of the day for bonus points. just kidding):

What helped, and what didn’t? Name the feature that lowered CV RMSE the most and the one that disappointed you most. Offer a reason for each.
Read one coefficient twice. Choose a variable in your final model. Give its β̂ reading and its ŷ reading in one sentence each.
What’s still missing? Look at your final residual map. Name one thing about those places you’d want to measure next, and where you might get the data.
How much of the remaining error might be uncertainty or statistical noise? Use your last plot.

Your answer: Among the spatial features, distance to the nearest High Speed station (the SPETA metro station) helped most, reducing CV RMSE from 12.38 to 10.60 percentage points; it may capture transit access that the ACS predictors miss. Regional Rail distance lowers RMSE by only about 0.03 points. Its information may overlap with other predictors. Adding a squared High Speed distance term further improved prediction, yielding a final RMSE of 9.53, about 23% below the baseline. Log-transforming bike density, by contrast, worsened performance.
The income coefficient (\(\hat{\beta} = -1.73\)) indicates that, holding other predictors constant, a $10,000 increase in tract median household income is associated with a 1.73-percentage-point decrease in the share of households without a vehicle. For example, a tract with a median income of $60,000 is predicted to have a zero-vehicle share 1.73 points lower than an otherwise identical tract at $50,000.
The final residual map shows less overprediction in Northeast Philadelphia, but underprediction persists in parts of North Philadelphia and is more apparent in some northwestern tracts. As a next step, I would measure bus service frequency, since rail proximity misses another potentially important transit option. Archived SEPTA GTFS schedules, if available, could provide weekday departure counts.
The uncertainty plot shows no consistent increase in absolute residuals as ACS coefficients of variation rise. Several of the largest errors occur among relatively reliable estimates, and observations with very high CVs are sparse. Sampling uncertainty may contribute to the remaining error, but the plot cannot quantify its share. The persistent spatial patterns also suggest that omitted neighborhood characteristics warrant further investigation.

Rent plus or minus 35% * 1.645 = 58% of med_rentE is the range of uncertainty. If the model’s residual is within that range, it could be just noise.

WarningTwo different CVs



Week 3 CV = coefficient of variation: how noisy is one estimate? Today’s CV = cross-validation: how well does a model predict data it hasn’t seen? Same letters, unrelated ideas.



6A: One train/test split

set.seed(5080)
n <- nrow(tracts)
train_idx <- sample(1:n, size = 0.8 * n)

train_data <- tracts[train_idx, ]
test_data  <- tracts[-train_idx, ]

m2_train <- lm(med_rentE ~ med_incE + pct_renter + pct_ba + n_stations,
               data = train_data)

test_pred <- predict(m2_train, newdata = test_data)

rmse_train <- sqrt(mean(residuals(m2_train)^2))
rmse_test  <- sqrt(mean((test_data$med_rentE - test_pred)^2))

title: Week 6: Feature Engineering for Linear Regression
text:
Key Concepts

1. Feature engineering and linear models
Feature engineering changes the variables supplied to a model. Logs, squared terms, and interactions let linear regression represent relationships that a straight line in the original variables would miss.
\[
\hat y = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 x + \hat\beta_2 x^2
\]
This is still a linear regression: the model is linear in its coefficients, even though its relationship with \(x\) is curved.
The lecture evaluates each specification by cross-validation RMSE. A transformation needs to improve predictions on held-out data; a better training fit alone is not enough.


2. Build the predictors and keep the sample consistent
The baseline uses four predictors:








Variable
Meaning
Construction or unit




income
Median household income
Dollars


pct_renter
Share of households that rent
100 * hh_renterE / hh_totalE


bldg_age
Age based on median year structure built
2023 - yr_builtE


dist_ch_mi
Distance from tract geometry to City Hall
Feet divided by 5,280



In the wide ACS output, E identifies the estimate and M identifies the margin of error. The lecture renames rentE to rent and retains rentM as rent_moe.
city_hall <- st_sfc(
  st_point(c(-75.1636, 39.9526)),
  crs = 4326
) %>%
  st_transform(2272)

tracts <- tracts_raw %>%
  mutate(
    rent       = rentE,
    rent_moe   = rentM,
    income     = incomeE,
    bldg_age   = 2023 - yr_builtE,
    pct_renter = 100 * hh_renterE / hh_totalE,
    dist_ch_mi = as.numeric(st_distance(geometry, city_hall)) / 5280
  ) %>%
  select(GEOID, rent, rent_moe, income, bldg_age, pct_renter, dist_ch_mi) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(rent), !is.na(income),
    !is.na(bldg_age), !is.na(pct_renter)
  )
tracts_raw has already been transformed to EPSG:2272, whose units are feet. The City Hall point starts in EPSG:4326, with coordinates ordered as longitude, latitude, and is transformed to match.
st_distance() here measures the shortest distance between each tract polygon and the point. It does not measure distance from the tract centroid. A tract containing City Hall has distance zero.
The cleaned lecture sample contains 377 tracts. All specifications use these rows. If a later feature introduces missing or invalid values, handle them before comparing models and rebuild the folds if the sample changes.


3. Baseline model and fixed-fold cross-validation
f0 <- rent ~ income + pct_renter + bldg_age + dist_ch_mi
m0 <- lm(f0, data = tracts)
f0 stores the formula. lm() estimates the coefficients, and m0 stores the fitted model. predict(m0, newdata = ...) applies those coefficients to another dataset.
The lecture assigns each row to one of ten folds once:
set.seed(5080)
folds <- sample(rep(1:10, length.out = nrow(tracts)))

cv_rmse <- function(f, data, log_outcome = FALSE) {
  preds <- numeric(nrow(data))

  for (k in 1:10) {
    m <- lm(f, data = data[folds != k, ])
    p <- predict(m, newdata = data[folds == k, ])

    if (log_outcome) p <- exp(p)

    preds[folds == k] <- p
  }

  sqrt(mean((data$rent - preds)^2))
}

folds != k selects the nine training folds.
folds == k selects the held-out fold.
preds[folds == k] <- p puts predictions back into their original row positions.
After ten iterations, every row has one out-of-fold prediction.

\[
RMSE = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\hat y_i)^2}
\]
This helper computes one RMSE across all out-of-fold predictions. It does not take an unweighted average of ten separate fold RMSEs. RMSE has the same units as the outcome and gives more weight to large errors than mean absolute error does.
The function uses the external object folds, so every input dataset must preserve the original row count and order. Reordering the data changes which observations belong to each fold.
model_log <- tibble(
  model = "m0",
  added = "baseline",
  cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f0, tracts)
)
model_log is a record of the models tried. The word log in this name has nothing to do with a logarithmic transformation.


4. Log transformations and coefficient interpretation
A log compresses a long right tail. It also makes equal proportional changes in a predictor have equal distances on the transformed scale. In R, log() uses the natural logarithm, and exp() reverses it.
f_logx <- rent ~ log(income) + pct_renter + bldg_age + dist_ch_mi
m_logx <- lm(f_logx, data = tracts)
For this model, the coefficient on log(income) is about 502.18. Holding the other predictors constant, a 1% increase in income corresponds to about $5.02 higher predicted rent.








Model
Formula
Interpretation of \(\beta\), holding other variables constant




Level-level
y ~ x
+1 unit of X corresponds to +\(\beta\) units of Y


Level-log
y ~ log(x)
+1% in X corresponds to approximately +\(\beta/100\) units of Y


Log-level
log(y) ~ x
+1 unit of X corresponds to approximately \(100\beta\)% change in Y


Log-log
log(y) ~ log(x)
+1% in X corresponds to approximately \(\beta\)% change in Y



For level-log models, a proportional increase \(r\) in X gives the exact predicted change:
\[
\Delta\hat y = \beta\ln(1+r)
\]
b <- coef(m_logx)["log(income)"]
b / 100         # About $5.02 for a 1% income increase
b * log(1.10)   # About $47.86 for a 10% income increase
For log-level models, the exact percentage change in the exponentiated prediction for a one-unit increase in X is:
\[
100\left(e^\beta-1\right)\%
\]
The log-log income coefficient in the lecture is about 0.363. A 1% increase in income corresponds to approximately 0.363% higher predicted rent. This coefficient is an elasticity.

Zeros and log1p()
log(0)     # -Inf
log1p(0)   # 0
log1p(x)   # log(1 + x)
Counts such as crimes or 311 calls can include meaningful zeros. log1p() preserves those observations when transforming nonnegative counts. Its interpretation concerns x + 1, so the usual percentage interpretation for log(x) is less accurate near zero. Neither function makes arbitrary negative values suitable for logging.


Logging Y changes the prediction scale
f_logy <- log(rent) ~ log(income) + pct_renter + bldg_age + dist_ch_mi
cv_rmse(f_logy, tracts, log_outcome = TRUE)
Predictions from this model are on the log-rent scale. Apply exp() to each prediction before comparing it with observed rent in dollars. A log-scale RMSE of 0.188 cannot be compared with a dollar RMSE of 265, and exponentiating the final RMSE does not fix this.
Direct exponentiation does not generally recover the conditional mean of rent; it can underpredict that mean. The lecture uses the simple back-transformation for model comparisons and notes that bias corrections exist.
A skewed predictor does not violate a requirement that X be normally distributed. Linear regression has no such requirement. Use plots and CV to decide whether a log is useful.



5. Squared terms and changing slopes
f_sq <- rent ~ log(income) + pct_renter +
  bldg_age + I(bldg_age^2) + dist_ch_mi

m_sq <- lm(f_sq, data = tracts)
Keep both the original variable and its square. I() tells R to perform arithmetic inside the formula; ^ otherwise has a special formula meaning.
For the age component:
\[
\hat y = \cdots + \beta_1 age + \beta_2 age^2
\]
The slope depends on age:
\[
\frac{d\hat y}{d age} = \beta_1 + 2\beta_2 age
\]
The lecture estimates \(\beta_1\approx-28.004\) and \(\beta_2\approx0.1823\). The positive squared coefficient gives an upward-opening curve. The linear coefficient alone does not mean that rent falls by $28 for every additional year of age throughout the sample.
The turning point is:
\[
age^* = -\frac{\beta_1}{2\beta_2}
\]
b1 <- coef(m_sq)["bldg_age"]
b2 <- coef(m_sq)["I(bldg_age^2)"]

-b1 / (2 * b2)         # About 76.8 years
range(tracts$bldg_age) # 5 to 85 years
Check whether the turning point lies inside the observed range. A turning point outside that range does not establish an observed reversal. A quadratic also keeps curving outside the training range, so extrapolated predictions can become unreasonable.
The old-building pile-up in the lecture plot partly comes from Census coding of early construction years. Check coding limits before interpreting a concentration of observations as a housing-market pattern.


6. Categories, dummy variables, and reference groups
Use a categorical predictor for existing groups, such as zoning classes, or when a continuous relationship is better represented by distinct groups.
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    ring = case_when(
      dist_ch_mi < 2 ~ "Core",
      dist_ch_mi < 5 ~ "Inner",
      TRUE ~ "Outer"
    ),
    ring = factor(ring, levels = c("Core", "Inner", "Outer"))
  )
case_when() uses the first matching condition. The Inner group therefore contains distances from 2 up to, but not including, 5 miles. Core is the reference because it is the first specified factor level.
For numeric breakpoints, use cut():
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(renter_band = cut(
    pct_renter,
    breaks = c(0, 33, 66, 100),
    labels = c("Mostly owners", "Mixed", "Mostly renters"),
    include.lowest = TRUE
  ))
With an intercept and the usual treatment coding, R represents \(k\) categories using \(k-1\) dummy variables:



Ring
ringInner
ringOuter




Core
0
0


Inner
1
0


Outer
0
1



model.matrix(~ ring, data = st_drop_geometry(tracts))
In the lecture model, ringInner is about -122 and ringOuter is about -164. Holding the other predictors constant, predicted rent in Inner tracts is about $122 lower than in Core tracts, and predicted rent in Outer tracts is about $164 lower than in Core tracts. These coefficients are differences from Core, not rent levels.
tracts_r <- tracts %>%
  mutate(ring = relevel(ring, ref = "Outer"))
Changing the reference changes the coefficient comparisons while leaving predictions unchanged. Numeric IDs also need factor() when their numbers are labels; treating district codes 1 through 18 as a continuous predictor would impose a numerical slope across arbitrary codes.
Binning removes information. Distances of 2.1 and 4.9 miles both become Inner. In this example, replacing continuous distance with rings increased CV RMSE.


7. Interactions: different slopes by group
An additive category term shifts the intercept. An interaction allows the relationship with another predictor to vary by group.
f_int <- rent ~ log(income) * ring + pct_renter +
  bldg_age + I(bldg_age^2)
In an R formula:
x * group
# Expands to: x + group + x:group
Writing \(x=\ln(income)\), the relevant terms are:
\[
\hat y = \beta_0 + \beta_1x
+ \gamma_I D_I + \gamma_O D_O
+ \delta_I xD_I + \delta_O xD_O + \cdots
\]








Ring
Intercept, with other predictors set to zero
Slope on log income




Core
\(\beta_0\)
\(\beta_1\)


Inner
\(\beta_0+\gamma_I\)
\(\beta_1+\delta_I\)


Outer
\(\beta_0+\gamma_O\)
\(\beta_1+\delta_O\)



The lecture coefficients give these log-income slopes:

Core: 653.70.
Inner: \(653.70-219.10=434.60\).
Outer: \(653.70-244.42=409.28\).

The main log-income coefficient is the Core slope. Each interaction coefficient is a difference from that slope. With an interaction, the Outer-Core rent difference also depends on income: \(\gamma_O+\delta_Ox\).
Use interactions when the relationship or a plot suggests different slopes. Each additional group slope requires another coefficient estimated from the same sample.


8. District fixed effects
The lecture uses a district factor to allow separate intercepts for Philadelphia’s planning districts:
\[
y_{ig} = \alpha_g + \beta x_{ig} + \epsilon_{ig}
\]
\(\alpha_g\) is the intercept for district \(g\). It captures district-level differences left unexplained by the measured predictors, without identifying their individual causes.
tracts <- tracts %>%
  st_join(districts %>% select(district = dist_name), largest = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(district = factor(district))

f_fe <- rent ~ log(income) + pct_renter +
  bldg_age + I(bldg_age^2) + district
largest = TRUE assigns a tract crossing district boundaries to the district with the largest overlapping area. It assigns attributes to the tract rather than splitting it into pieces.
After adding district fixed effects, the log-income coefficient changes from about 519.74 to 427.39. The income relationship now uses variation within districts after controlling for their intercepts. Some of the earlier association reflected differences between districts.
Fixed effects do not account for every unmeasured difference within a district, and they do not turn an association into a causal effect. Residual maps can show whether geographic clusters remain after adding them.

Small groups and unseen factor levels
tracts %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(district) %>%
  arrange(n)
One lecture district has only one tract. When that tract is held out, the training set contains no observation from its district, so prediction encounters a factor level the model has never learned.
The lecture handles groups with fewer than ten observations by assigning their tracts to the district of the nearest tract in a sufficiently large group. It keeps the original district label and creates district_cv for the CV specification. This changes group membership; it does not dissolve or combine tract geometries.
Other options discussed include a coarser geography or pooling small groups into an Other category. A geographically sensible merge gives the resulting category a clearer meaning. About ten observations per group is a classroom rule of thumb for ten-fold CV, not a guarantee that every training fold will contain every category.



9. R syntax to remember







Code
Purpose or check




log(x)
Natural log; requires positive values for finite results


log1p(x)
Compute log(1 + x); accommodates zero counts


exp(pred)
Back-transform a log prediction


x + I(x^2)
Include a linear term and its square


factor(x)
Treat labels as categories


relevel(x, ref = "...")
Choose a reference category


case_when() / cut()
Construct categories from conditions or breakpoints


x * group
Include both main effects and their interaction


model.matrix()
Inspect the encoded predictors


count(group)
Check group sizes before CV


st_join(..., largest = TRUE)
Assign the spatial match with the largest overlap


add_row()
Record another model and its CV RMSE

title: Week 7: Spatial Errors and House Price Prediction
text:
Key Concepts

1. Residuals
A residual is the actual value minus the predicted value:
\[
e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i
\]

Positive residual: the model underpredicts.
Negative residual: the model overpredicts.

For example, if a house sells for $240,000 and the model predicts $285,000, the residual is −$45,000. The model overpredicts by $45,000.


2. Buffer Counts and kNN Distances
Buffer counts and kNN distances describe nearby conditions in different ways.








Feature
What is fixed?
What is measured?




Buffer count
Search radius
Number of events inside the radius


Mean kNN distance
Number of nearby events
Average distance to those events



Two houses may both have zero crimes within a buffer but differ substantially in their distance to the nearest crimes. The kNN feature captures that difference.
Use an appropriate projected CRS and check its units. 660 feet equals 1/8 mile.


3. Spatial Lag and Spatial Weights
A spatial lag summarizes values at neighboring locations. With equally weighted, row-standardized neighbors, it is the average of their values.
For four neighbors with residuals of +40, +20, −10, and −30 thousand dollars:
\[
\text{Spatial lag} = \frac{40 + 20 - 10 - 30}{4} = 5
\]
The average neighboring residual is +$5,000.
Spatial lag refers to a spatial relationship, not a previous time period. Results depend on the neighbor definition and weighting method.
In this lesson, kNN serves two purposes:

Finding nearby crime incidents to construct a predictor.
Finding nearby houses to diagnose residual patterns.



4. Moran’s I
Moran’s I measures spatial association. Applied to residuals, it asks whether neighboring houses tend to have similar deviations from the mean residual.

Above the random baseline: similar residuals tend to cluster.
Near the random baseline: little overall spatial association under the chosen weights.
Below the random baseline: neighboring residuals tend to differ.

Residual clustering can suggest omitted local information, an unsuitable model form, or data problems. It does not establish a specific cause.
Moran’s I is neither prediction error in dollars nor the percentage of variation explained. Comparisons require consistent samples and spatial weights.


5. Permutation Testing
A permutation test evaluates whether the observed spatial association is unusual under random assignment of values to locations.
The procedure is:

Keep locations and spatial weights fixed.
Randomly reassign the observed residuals across locations.
Recalculate Moran’s I.
Repeat and compare the observed statistic with the simulated distribution.

With nsim = 499, the function performs 499 permutations. It does not refit the regression 499 times.
A small upper-tail p-value indicates that the observed Moran’s I is unusually large under the specified randomization null. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.


6. Cross-Validation and RMSE
Cross-validation (CV) evaluates predictions on observations temporarily excluded from model fitting.
In ten-fold CV:

Divide the training data into ten folds.
Train on nine folds and predict the remaining fold.
Repeat until every fold has been held out once.
Summarize the held-out prediction errors.

CV RMSE measures prediction-error magnitude in the outcome’s units. Moran’s I measures the spatial structure of errors.
A model can have little spatial clustering while still making large prediction errors. Compare models using the same observations and CV folds.


7. Target Leakage
Target leakage occurs when held-out outcome information enters model training or feature construction.
For example, calculating neighboring mean sale prices from all observed prices before splitting CV folds can allow validation outcomes to enter features.
For this task, construct spatial predictors from available environmental information, such as crime exposure or transit access, rather than neighboring target prices.
Neighboring residual averages contain outcome information. They are useful for diagnosis but should not be reused as ordinary prediction features.


8. Improving and Evaluating the Model
Spatial error patterns can motivate additional features:







Suspected issue
Possible model change




Missing local amenities or disamenities
Add accessibility, distance, or buffer features


Overall differences between neighborhoods
Add neighborhood fixed effects


Relationships that vary across places
Add interaction terms


Nonlinear relationships
Add log transformations or polynomial terms



Evaluate changes using CV RMSE, residual maps, and Moran’s I. A lower training error or smaller Moran’s I alone does not establish better prediction.
Select the model using training-set CV, refit it on the available training data, and predict every required test observation. The separate test set provides the final independent evaluation.

title: Week 8: Local Moran’s I and LISA
text:
Last week, global Moran’s I on the residuals told us whether the model’s errors cluster. As the model improves, that number should fall. But a single number cannot tell us where the problems are. This week we broke it apart, one house at a time.

Reviewed global Moran’s I on residuals as a diagnostic to track across model versions.
Worked through a five-house example by hand: residual, deviation from the mean, neighbors’ average deviation, and local Moran’s I.
Classified each location into one of four quadrants (HH, HL, LH, LL) and interpreted them as prediction errors.
Discussed why a LISA value must be read together with its quadrant, its significance, the size of the errors, and a map.
Odds and ends: the RealPage case on algorithmic rent pricing.

Discussed why a LISA value must be read together with its quadrant, its significance, the size of the errors, and a map.
Odds and ends: the RealPage case on algorithmic rent pricing.

title: Week 8: Local Moran’s I and LISA
text:
Key Concepts

1. From Global to Local
Global Moran’s I asks: across the whole study area, do similar residuals sit next to each other?
Local Moran’s I, a LISA (Local Indicator of Spatial Association; Anselin, 1995), asks: does this particular location resemble its neighbors?
With row-standardized weights, the global statistic is the average of the local ones:
\[
I = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} I_i
\]
LISA is therefore a decomposition of the global statistic, not a separate idea.


2. The Formula
Let \(z_i = e_i - \bar{e}\) be the deviation of location \(i\)’s residual from the mean residual, and
\[
m_2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} z_i^2
\]
Then
\[
I_i = \frac{z_i}{m_2}\sum_{j} w_{ij} z_j
\]
The sum \(\sum_j w_{ij} z_j\) is the spatial lag of \(z\). With row-standardized weights, it is the neighbors’ average deviation.
\(I_i\) is large and positive when location \(i\) and its neighbors deviate strongly in the same direction. It is negative when they deviate in opposite directions.


3. Worked Example: Five Houses in a Row
Houses A–E sit on a line, and each house’s neighbors are the houses directly next to it. All values are in thousands of dollars.
The mean residual is \((100 + 80 + 20 - 50 - 70)/5 = 16\), so \(z_i = e_i - 16\).

4. The Four Quadrants (Moran Scatterplot)
The Moran scatterplot places \(z_i\) on the x-axis and its spatial lag on the y-axis. Each quadrant describes a different pattern:

Positive \(I_i\): a cluster (HH or LL).

The sign alone cannot distinguish HH from LL. The quadrant is needed.


5. Reading the Quadrants as Errors
When the variable is a residual, “high” and “low” have a specific meaning:
\[
e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i
\]
A high residual means the model underpredicted; a low residual means it overpredicted.

HH: a pocket of underprediction. The model consistently guesses too low here. The area may be worth more than the features suggest because of an unmeasured amenity, a gentrifying block, or a strong school catchment.
LL: a pocket of overprediction. The model consistently guesses too high. Something the model does not see may be pulling prices down, such as vacancy, blight, a nearby disamenity, or a data issue.
HL / LH: isolated surprises. A single house does not match its neighbors, such as a renovated house on a distressed block, a teardown on an expensive block, or a bad record.

Strictly speaking, “high” and “low” are relative to the mean residual, not to zero. With OLS and an intercept, the mean residual is zero on the training data, so the two coincide. They can differ on test data or after filtering.


6. Reading LISA in Context
A LISA value on its own is not an answer. Read it together with:

The quadrant: a positive \(I_i\) could be HH or LL, which represent opposite problems for the model.
Significance: a conditional permutation test keeps location \(i\)’s value fixed, randomly reassigns the remaining values to its neighbors, and recalculates \(I_i\). Cluster maps usually show only significant locations.
The size of the residuals: a strong LL cluster of small overpredictions matters less than a weak cluster of $100,000 errors. LISA measures pattern; CV RMSE and MAE measure magnitude.
A map: the cluster map, with quadrant colors and non-significant locations in grey, shows where the patterns are.

Cautions:

Multiple testing. With thousands of houses, roughly 5% may appear significant at \(p < 0.05\) by chance alone. Use a stricter cutoff or a false discovery rate (FDR) correction before drawing strong conclusions.
Neighbor definitions matter. Results change with the spatial weights, such as kNN with \(k = 5\) versus \(k = 10\), contiguity, or distance bands. Report the choice.
Clusters are not causes. An LL cluster shows where the model fails, not why. It indicates where to look for a missing feature.



7. Using LISA to Improve the Model
The cluster map can become a feature-engineering checklist:







What the map shows
Possible next step




HH cluster (underprediction)
Look for a missing amenity: parks, transit, school quality, or a neighborhood fixed effect


LL cluster (overprediction)
Look for a missing disamenity: vacancy, crime, industrial land, or flood risk


Clusters that follow neighborhood boundaries
Add neighborhood fixed effects


Scattered HL / LH outliers
Check for data errors, non-arm’s-length sales, or unusual properties



After adding features, rerun global Moran’s I and the LISA map, and compare CV RMSE using the same folds. A useful change should shrink the clusters without worsening out-of-sample error.


8. R Workflow
library(sf)
library(spdep)

# Residuals from the fitted model
sales$resid <- residuals(model)

# Neighbors: five nearest houses, row-standardized
coords <- st_coordinates(sales)
nb <- knn2nb(knearneigh(coords, k = 5))
lw <- nb2listw(nb, style = "W")

# Global Moran's I (last week)
moran.mc(sales$resid, lw, nsim = 499)

# Local Moran's I with a conditional permutation test
lisa <- localmoran_perm(sales$resid, lw, nsim = 499)

sales$Ii   <- lisa[, "Ii"]
sales$p    <- lisa[, "Pr(z != E(Ii)) Sim"]
sales$quad <- attr(lisa, "quadr")$mean   # High-High, Low-Low, High-Low, Low-High

# Keep only significant locations for the cluster map
sales$cluster <- ifelse(sales$p < 0.05, as.character(sales$quad), "Not significant")

section: Odds and Ends: The RealPage Case
text:
Odds and Ends: The RealPage Case
RealPage sells revenue-management software that recommends daily rents to landlords. In August 2024, the DOJ and several states sued the company, alleging that the software pooled competing landlords’ nonpublic data and pushed them toward aligned, higher rents (“algorithmic collusion”).
In November 2025, the DOJ announced a proposed settlement with no fines and no admission of wrongdoing. Under its terms, RealPage must:

Stop using competitors’ nonpublic data for real-time recommendations; training data must be at least a year old.
Remove features that discouraged rent decreases or aligned prices among competitors.
Stop hyper-local pricing.

Several states that had joined the suit were not part of the settlement, and a number of cities, including Philadelphia, have passed their own ordinances restricting rent-setting algorithms.
Why this case belongs in a policy analytics course:

A pricing model becomes a public-policy actor once enough of the market relies on it.
The central issue is less the algorithm itself than the data it is allowed to see. This is the same question as target leakage, scaled up to an entire market.
Our house-price models ask, “What is this home worth?” RealPage’s model asks, “What can this landlord charge?” The tools are similar, but the consequences are very different.

title: Assignment 5: House Price Prediction, Chicago
text:
Part 6: Reflection
Location was the most useful source of improvement. Adding Ward effects and allowing the building-area coefficient to vary across Wards substantially reduced prediction error. The final North/South adjustment then allowed the relationship between lot area and price to differ across two broad regions. It improved RMSE and reduced negative predictions without requiring a separate regression for every neighborhood. These are predictive associations, not proof that geography itself causes the price differences.
The model comparisons also show why RMSE alone is insufficient. Ward-specific lot-area slopes achieved a lower error but generated an extreme negative test prediction. We preferred the broader North/South adjustment, which produced fewer negative values. Nevertheless, two negative test predictions remain, and unusual houses are still difficult to value. Valid expensive and old houses were retained because removing them would change the population being predicted.
The full-bathroom coefficient is $49,509. Holding the other predictors fixed, one additional full bathroom changes the fitted price by this amount. This does not measure the causal return from adding a bathroom: interior condition, renovation and other unrecorded features may also explain the association.
The equity results are less encouraging. Although NS improves overall dollar accuracy, the lowest-income group’s median valuation ratio and overvalued share increase slightly relative to m10. We therefore cannot describe the final model as an improvement in assessment fairness. If used for taxation, its remaining proportional errors could place excess burden on owners of lower-valued homes.
We would use these predictions to support review, not to set tax bills directly. Additional condition data may help, but any changes should be assessed using both accuracy and income-group diagnostics. Repeated comparisons on the same folds can make the chosen CV result optimistic. Hidden test prices provide a separate check, while prediction for future years would require time-based validation.

text: We used residential burglaries in Philadelphia to introduce count regression and discuss the limitations of predictive policing. The exercise used 2024 crime and 311 records to build features for predicting 2025 burglary counts, then compared the model with a kernel density baseline.

title: Week 9: Predictive Policing
text:
Key Concepts

1. Fishnets and the Unit of Analysis
Crime incidents are points, so we need spatial units in which to count them. A fishnet divides the city into 500 × 500 ft cells, with each cell becoming one observation. Equal-sized cells make spatial counts easier to compare, although the choice of grid size still affects the patterns.
The exercise used EPSG:2272, where distances are measured in feet. Always check the CRS before creating grids or calculating distances.


2. Why Use Poisson Regression?
Burglary counts are nonnegative integers, and most cells contain zero burglaries. OLS can produce negative predictions and may poorly represent the relationship between the mean and variance.
Poisson regression models the expected count through a log link:
\[
\log(\lambda_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \cdots
\]
Exponentiating the linear predictor keeps expected counts positive. Predictions can be fractional because they represent averages, rather than individual observed counts.
For an unlogged predictor, \(e^\beta\) is the multiplicative change in expected count for a one-unit increase. For example, \(\beta = 0.20\) implies approximately 22% more expected burglaries, holding other predictors constant.


3. Overdispersion
Poisson assumes that the conditional variance equals the conditional mean. If variability exceeds what the model allows, the data are overdispersed. Negative binomial regression adds a dispersion parameter and can accommodate this additional variation.


4. Spatial Features and Leakage
The exercise constructed several types of predictors:







Feature type
Example




Count within a cell
Number of abandoned-vehicle reports


Nearest distance
Distance to the closest streetlight outage


kNN distance
Average distance to the three nearest graffiti reports


Distance to a fixed location
Distance to City Hall


Distance to a hotspot
Distance to a previous-year LISA High–High cluster



Features must be available at the time of prediction. Building hotspots from 2025 burglaries to predict those same burglaries would leak the outcome into the predictors. Using 2024 records avoids that particular leakage.


5. Compare Against a Simple Baseline
A more complicated model should be compared with a KDE map of previous-year burglaries. One classroom comparison measured the share of 2025 burglaries captured within the highest-ranked 10% of cells.
This asks a practical question: does the model identify future concentrations better than simply smoothing last year’s crime locations? A fair assessment also requires held-out evaluation.

title: Week 9: Predictive Policing
text:
Policy Discussion
Recorded crime reflects what happens, what people report, and what police record. Reporting rates, trust in police, and enforcement practices vary across neighborhoods. Officer-generated records, such as drug-possession arrests, are especially sensitive to patrol locations.
This creates a feedback loop: a model identifies an area, more officers are deployed there, more incidents are recorded, and those records reinforce the model’s prediction. The 311 predictors also reflect residents’ willingness and ability to report problems.
Cross-validation cannot resolve this measurement problem when both training and test data contain the same bias. Predicting police records accurately does not necessarily mean predicting actual crime accurately or allocating patrols fairly.

So there is a trade-off: the single most predictive variable is also the one that carries the most race information, because past arrests reflect where police patrol and who they stop. Removing it buys some fairness in error rates at a large cost in accuracy, and still leaves a gap.

NoteTakeaways




Leaving race out is not the same as being fair. Priors and age are correlated with race, so the race-blind model still gives Black defendants about twice the false positive rate of white defendants.
Calibration and equal error rates can’t both hold here. When base rates differ, you can’t satisfy both fairness definitions at once; choosing between them is a policy decision, not a technical one.
The data carries the history. priors_count is the strongest predictor and also the clearest channel for race, because arrest records reflect policing patterns, not just behavior.

The scenario
The Georgia Department of Community Supervision is considering a risk model to guide parole decisions. Every person released to parole would get a predicted probability of being rearrested within three years. The department has two proposed uses:

Use A: people above a threshold get more restrictive supervision (more check-ins, electronic monitoring, faster revocation).
Use B: people above a threshold get priority for reentry services (housing assistance, job placement, a case manager).

The department has promised that the model will not use race. You’ve been hired to build it and to tell them whether that promise means what they think it means.
What you’re turning in: this rendered document, published in the assignments/ folder of your portfolio.
How this assignment works: it has less scaffolding than earlier ones. The Week 11 lab (COMPAS) is your fully worked example: almost every step here has a matching step there.       share_flagged = mean(flag),

      specificity  = sum(flag == 0 & recid == 0) / sum(recid == 0),
      # of the people flagged, the share who were actually rearrested
      precision    = sum(flag == 1 & recid == 1) / sum(flag == 1),
      accuracy     = mean(flag == recid)
    )
}

Age carries most of it. Black parolees are younger at release: 33% are 18–27, compared to 22% of white parolees, and 52% vs. 41% are under 33. Your memo:

To: Deputy Commissioner, Georgia Department of Community Supervision From: Xuanyu Zhou Re: Thresholds for the parole risk model, and what “race-blind” does and doesn’t mean
The model gives each person released to parole a score: the estimated chance of being rearrested within three years. I tested it on 7,807 past parolees it had never seen. It ranks people reasonably well. Given one person who was rearrested and one who wasn’t, it scores the rearrested person higher 71% of the time. But it makes two kinds of mistakes. A false positive labels someone high risk who would not have been rearrested. A false negative labels someone low risk who would have been. A cutoff, the score above which we act, trades one mistake for the other, so the right cutoff depends on what we’re doing with it.
Use A, more restrictive supervision: cutoff 0.70. Here a false positive is serious: a person who would have stayed out of trouble gets electronic monitoring, more check-ins and faster revocation, which can send them back to prison for a technical violation. A false negative is less costly, because it means standard supervision, which is what everyone gets today. At 0.70 the model flags about 31% of parolees, and roughly three of every four people it flags were in fact rearrested. Only about 17% of people who would not have been rearrested get flagged, compared with 53% at the default cutoff of 0.50. The cost is that it misses about 6 in 10 people who are rearrested.
Use B, priority for reentry services: cutoff 0.50. Here the costs flip. A false positive means someone who would have been fine gets housing help or a case manager. That costs money, but harms no one. A false negative means someone who needed help, and went on to be rearrested, didn’t get it. At 0.50 the model reaches 82% of the people who will be rearrested. The catch is scale: it flags about 70% of all parolees, so this cutoff only works if the budget can serve that many. If it can’t, a higher cutoff rations services to fewer people, and the department should say openly that it is choosing whom to leave out.
Does “the model doesn’t use race” mean it treats Black and white parolees the same? No. Black and white parolees in our data are rearrested at nearly the same rate (58% vs. 56%). Yet at 0.50, among people who were not rearrested, the model wrongly flags 57% of Black parolees and 48% of white parolees. At 0.70 that becomes 18% vs. 15%. Fewer people are wrongly flagged overall, but Black parolees still carry about 1.2 times the burden at every cutoff I tested. Race gets in through other information. Mainly it’s age: Black parolees in this data are younger at release, and age is the model’s strongest predictor. When I removed age, the gap nearly disappeared, but the model became much less accurate. Leaving race out is a promise about what goes in; it says nothing about who gets the mistakes.
In practice: report false positive rates by race at least yearly, never let a high score alone trigger a revocation, and keep a person reviewing every Use A decision.
I would deploy this for Use B, unless the same scores are also used to tighten supervision under Use A without a cutoff of at least 0.70 and a yearly check of false positive rates by race.
